title: Compact join tables and normalize lookup refs to reduce control-plane join amplification
creator: Marco Chen
description:
Background:
Our control-plane OLTP workload shows sustained high p95 latency on tenant-scoped read paths. Root cause analysis points to repeated wide JOINs between event_history, tenant_refs, and shared_lookup tables where skewed tenant cardinalities and redundant lookup columns cause amplification. Several legacy denormalized columns were added over the years for fast reads; these now cause bloat and force sequential plans on the primary DB.

Goal:
1) Reduce typical tenant read latency by 30-50% for high-cardinality tenants.
2) Reduce storage and VACUUM pressure from duplicated lookup columns.
3) Make schema changes with zero downtime and reversible migrations.

Scope:
- Normalize shared lookup references into a compact lookup_id table (lookup_compact) and replace repeated textual columns with small integer FK refs where safe.
- Create partial and covering indexes for tenant-scoped hot queries (tenant_id + status + created_at ranges).
- Introduce online, chunked backfill jobs using replica-based reads and concurrent index creation to avoid locks.
- Deprecate two legacy denormalized columns on event_history after validation and offer a 30-day mirror window before drop.

Non-goals:
- Major data model redesign for billing or usage aggregation tables (these will be separate RFCs).
acceptance_criteria: Median and p95 read latency for tenant-scoped GET /tenants/{id}/events reduced by >=30% in canary region
Query plans for top-10 hot queries show index seeks rather than seq scans on production sample workload
Backfill completes in controlled chunks without causing replica lag above configured threshold
Migration runbook tested in staging and run once in a low-traffic canary prior to global rollout
Feature flags present to route a percentage of traffic to new index paths for verification
plan: Phase 0: Read-only analysis and mocks (2 days) - collect explain plans and build synthetic replay of tenant-heavy workload
Phase 1: Add compact lookup table and insert-only change (no schema swap) - create table lookup_compact and populate from existing shared_lookup via idempotent inserts (concurrent) (3 days)
Phase 2: Add FK columns (nullable) to event_history and tenant_refs, deploy code to write both denorm + fk (feature gated) (2 days)
Phase 3: Backfill FK values in small chunks using a background worker reading from read replica; monitor replica lag and CPU (estimated 4-7 days depending on canary throughput)
Phase 4: Add partial covering indexes concurrently tuned for tenant-scoped patterns (CONCURRENTLY where DB supports). Validate query plans in canary region (2 days)
Phase 5: Switch reads to prefer FK paths via query hints or route-level feature flag. Monitor latency/cost for 72 hours (1 day)
Phase 6: Deprecate and mirror denormalized columns: keep writes for 30 days while reads migrate. After 30 days and validation, remove columns in a guarded migration (3 days)
Phase 7: Post-mortem and metrics dashboard update; add long-term retention policy for compact lookup table if needed (1 day)
migration_steps: 1) Create lookup_compact with columns (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, lookup_key TEXT UNIQUE, canonical_value TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMP) on replica promotion-safe DDL node
2) Populate lookup_compact by deduplicating shared_lookup rows in batches of 10k, insert ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
3) Add nullable fk columns to event_history and tenant_refs (using ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN) - low-risk because nullable
4) Deploy application change to write both denormalized column and fk when creating/updating records (feature-flagged), no reads changed
5) Run background backfill worker reading from replica, updating primary in controlled window of 5000 rows per job with exponential backoff on errors

6) Create partial indexes CONCURRENTLY for tenant-scoped filters: e.g., CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_event_history_tenant_status_created_at ON event_history (tenant_id, status, created_at) WHERE created_at > now() - interval '90 days'
7) Route 5-10% of traffic to new query path and collect traces, then ramp to 50% before full switch
8) After 30-day mirror window and verification, drop denormalized columns with online-aware DROP COLUMN (and reindex if necessary)
rollback_plan:
If any phase causes unacceptable replica lag (> configured threshold) or latency regressions >10% vs baseline:
- Pause backfill jobs immediately via orchestration control plane.
- Disable feature flag so application writes stop populating FK; existing writes remain stable.
- If an index creation causes issues, cancel the operation if possible and fallback to previous read path.
- Run quick rollback migration to mark fk columns as ignored by new code paths until we can remediate.
- If storage bloat unexpectedly increases, revert by truncating undo table populated by backfill (we keep backfill delta logs for 48 hours).
risks_and_mitigation: Replica lag during backfill - mitigate by small chunk sizes, off-peak windows, and adaptive concurrency
Index creation still pressures I/O - mitigate by tuning maintenance_work_mem and spreading operations across replicas
Application bugs on dual-write - mitigate with feature flags, canary traffic, and automations to compare denorm vs fk values
Rollback complexity if FK partially applied - mitigation: keep idempotent backfill jobs and detailed audit logs per batch
observability: Add dashboards: backfill progress, batch job success rate, replica lag by region, index usage (pg_stat_user_indexes) and top seq scans
Add alert: replica lag > 30s for more than 2 minutes during migration window
Add query-level tracing for canary traffic with sampling to identify regressions

2026-02-23 | Sana Ibrahim (DB Infra): Recommend increasing maintenance_work_mem during index creation windows and creating indexes during low-traffic hours. Also suggested toggling autovacuum settings temporarily.

2026-02-28 | Aisha Patel: Deployed feature-flagged dual-writes to canary region (eu-west). Observed 38% p95 improvement on canary tenant set after partial index creation. Preparing global rollout plan.
